newsitem.title: UK: Full text of Dec UK purchasing managers' survey.
newsitem.headline: Full text of Dec UK purchasing managers' survey.

text.p: Following is the full text of the December Report on Business (Purchasing Managers' Survey) of the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS):
MANUFACTURING OUTPUT CONTINUES TO RISE IN RESPONSE TO ORDER BOOK GROWTH. CHEAPER IMPORTS DRIVE INPUT PRICES LOWER AGAIN.

The Purchasing Managers' Index* signalled expansion of the manufacturing economy for the seventh month running in December as both output and employment rose to meet further improvements in order books.

However, although order levels rose on the whole, driven by an acceleration in the rate of growth of demand for both consumer goods and capital goods, the PMI was weakened by a modest deceleration in the overall rate of growth of order books which was in turn due to two principal factors.
First, the stronger pound led to weaker growth in export markets for the second month in a row.

Second, December saw a greater incidence of deliberate destocking designed to meet year-end inventory targets: stocks of purchases showed the largest monthly fall in four years as firms reduced their monthly purchases of goods to be used in the production process. As a result, producers of components (who generally supply inputs to producers of consumer and capital goods) reported a deceleration in order book growth.

The PMI was also weakened by an easing in the rate of growth of output. This easing was again closely linked to deliberate destocking policies, often designed to meet year-end inventory targets, as firms chose to restrict output growth below the rate of growth of orders. Stocks of finished goods showed the sharpest monthly fall for nearly three years as a consequence.

Despite the need to run down stock levels, employment rose (albeit modestly) during the month in order to boost production capacity to meet future growth of orders. This was the fifth consecutive monthly rise in employment.

Finally, prices paid by purchasing managers fell sharply again and have now fallen continually for fourteen months. Some upward price pressures have been reported in recent months as demand has hardened and suppliers have become busier. Suppliers' delivery times lengthened modestly for the fourth month running. However, these upward pressures were more than offset by the deflationary effect of sterling's strength as manufacturers benefited from cheaper imported inputs.

* The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is a composite indicator designed to provide an overall view of activity in the manufacturing economy and acts as a leading indicator for the whole economy. The indicator is derived from individual diffusion indices which measure changes in output, new orders, employment, suppliers' delivery times and stocks of goods purchased. A reading of the PMI below 50% indicates that the manufacturing economy is generally declining; above 50%, that it is generally expanding. The seasonally adjusted index may be subject to revision as improved estimation of seasonal adjustments occur with each month's new data.
OUTPUT

The Output Index signalled a further overall increase in December as production of consumer, capital and intermediate goods all rose to meet higher order levels. The monthly increase in output was less than that seen over the previous three months, but this deceleration could in part be attributed to stronger than usual seasonal effects, such as depletion of finished goods' stock in preparation for year-end stock taking.
NEW ORDERS

New orders rose strongly again in December, the seventh consecutive monthly rise, with consumer goods again reporting the sharpest improvement. Producers of both consumer and intermediate goods (components) reported some difficulties in export markets due to the rise in the value of sterling since the summer, but export orders nevertheless increased on the whole compared with the previous month.
QUANTITY OF PURCHASES

The quantity of goods purchased for use in production fell very slightly in December, the first such fall since July. The decline was largely attributable to both weaker output growth and a stronger than usual seasonal effort by purchasing managers to reduce stocks of materials for cost considerations in advance of the year end.
PRICES

The Prices Index fell again, signalling sharply lower prices than a month ago. Higher fuel prices were widely reported and some domestic suppliers were reported to have pushed prices higher in the light of growing demand. However, on the whole surplus capacity continued to drive price competition for inputs while the appreciation of sterling since the summer further reduced the cost of imported goods and raw materials.
SUPPLIERS' DELIVERY TIMES

The seasonally adjusted Suppliers' Delivery Times Index remained below 50.0 in December, recording a lengthening of delivery times for the fourth consecutive month. Longer delivery times have simply reflected increased demand, meaning suppliers have been busier. However, supply delays were not widespread and were reported by only 8% of the survey panel.
STOCKS OF PURCHASES

The seasonally adjusted Stocks of Purchases Index for December recorded the sharpest single monthly fall in raw material stock holdings for four years. Purchasing managers were commonly reported to have deliberately held back on purchasing goods in order to allow stocks to fall to meet inventory targets, while an increase in the rate of production during the month further depleted supplies.
STOCKS OF FINISHED GOODS

Purchasing managers continued to reduce stocks of finished goods for cost considerations in December, with additional efforts often being made to meet year-end stock taking targets. Inventories of consumer, investment and intermediary goods all fell again as the effects of these deliberate policies were exaggerated by depletion through high sales. Stocks showed the largest monthly fall since February 1994 as a result.
EMPLOYMENT

The seasonally adjusted Employment Index signalled the fifth modest consecutive monthly increase in December. Recruitment by both consumer and capital goods producers to meet order book growth was in part offset by job shedding in the intermediate industries (mainly component manufacturers).
CONSUMER GOODS

On the whole producers of consumer goods remained upbeat in December, reporting that, despite some problems in export markets due to the strength of sterling, new orders showed very strong growth again (the sharpest monthly rise since June). Employment was also increased in order to boost capacity. Output of consumer goods rose again as a result, but at a much reduced rate of growth compared with recent months. The strong growth in orders suggests that this decrease in the rate of growth is likely to be temporary, largely reflecting stronger than usual seasonal effects such as a greater than normal incidence of stock reduction. Stocks of both purchases and finished goods were deliberately reduced before year end stock taking.
INVESTMENT/CAPITAL GOODS

Producers of capital (investment) goods saw a significant improvement in order levels in December, with export demand holding up particularly well in the face of the stronger pound. Employment was increased during the month to raise production capacity in line with the growth of demand (output expanded for the fourth month running), but sales nevertheless outstripped production and stocks of finished goods dropped sharply as a result. The amount of materials purchased for use in production fell, but this was partly attributable to a larger than usual effort to deplete stocks to meet year end targets. Prices paid for inputs fell again, but delivery times showed the first lengthening since 1995 as some suppliers had difficulty meeting short term demand requirements.
INTERMEDIATE GOODS

Output of intermediate goods (components) rose for the seventh month running in December, having fallen throughout most of the first half of the year. New orders rose again, although to a lesser extent than in previous recent months. Slower growth of orders was partly attributable to weaker export demand due to the appreciation of sterling in the second half of the year, but was also a reflection of destocking by customers. More materials were bought to meet output growth, with some suppliers having to lengthen delivery times to meet orders. Any upwards pressures on prices arising from higher demand were checked by the strength of sterling, which reduced the cost of many imported goods and led to an overall fall in prices.
-- Richard Murphy, London Newsroom 44 171 542 2774
